item.title: Meta says strengthened systems, deployed new LLMs to prevent, detect CSAM
item.description: Meta says a dedicated language model, AI sweeps and a red-teaming agent will help detect harmful ads, identify gaps in its defences and stop banned users returning ...
item.dc:creator: Aashish Aryan
item.content:encoded: Social media giant Meta on Wednesday said it has improved its child sexual abuse material (CSAM) detection systems to improve the “efficacy” of its systems in preventing such content from being posted across its platforms. The company listed a series of improvements, such as deploying a new large language model (LLM) to flag advertising content that may look relatively harmless but shows indicators of redirecting users to illegal and harmful content off Meta’s platforms. In a blog post, Meta said that while it continued to detect, investigate and remove CSAM from its platforms, bad actors had resorted to newer methods, such as using advertisements to redirect people to other third-party platforms. “Once we understood the design of this malicious advertising scheme, we didn’t stop at the ones reported to us. We widened our investigation to find related activity across our platforms, disabled the violating accounts behind it, and blocked the off-platform links involved,” the company said in a blog post. In addition to deploying the dedicated LLM, Meta has also launched new artificial intelligence (AI)-driven “sweeps of ad content” to look for child sexual abuse and exploitative material that its systems did not catch, the company said in the blog post. A red-teaming AI agent has also been deployed by the company to find loopholes in Meta’s defences against CSAM, so that these weaknesses can be found and corrected, the company said. Meta has also strengthened its systems for identifying bad actors who try to return to its platforms after their accounts are removed, the blog post said. These actions by the social media conglomerate come within a month of the company’s top executives being summoned by the Indian government over alleged failures to contain CSAM and allowing advertisements that promoted such material across its platforms. Last month, Meta became the first social media platform to agree to share details of CSAM cases and repeat offenders with Indian law enforcement agencies. Until then, all US-headquartered social media platforms, including Meta, shared instances of CSAM only with the National Centre for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC), a private US non-profit organisation. The NCMEC would then share the details of repeat offenders or other such online accounts with the law enforcement agencies in their respective domains. Google soon followed suit and said that it would also start sharing these details with Indian law enforcement agencies.

item.title: MFs, advisers adopt 'wait-and-watch' stance on duration after RBI rate rise
item.description: Debt fund managers and wealth advisers favour accruals and shorter-duration bonds, awaiting clarity on inflation and peak policy rates before adding duration exposure ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / MFs, advisers adopt 'wait-and-watch' stance on duration after RBI rate rise

MFs, advisers adopt 'wait-and-watch' stance on duration after RBI rate rise Debt fund managers and wealth advisers favour accruals and shorter-duration bonds, awaiting clarity on inflation and peak policy rates before adding duration exposure

Debt mutual fund managers are turning cautious on longer-duration bonds as the RBI begins its rate-hike cycle. (Representative Image)

Abhishek Kumar Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 11:23 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Debt fund managers struck a cautious note on government bonds, particularly longer-duration securities, following the announcements by the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) on Wednesday. The policy, delivered against the backdrop of persistent global risks, marked the beginning of a rate-hike cycle that fund managers believe could cumulatively amount to 100 basis points (bps) or more.   A rise in interest rates is negative for bonds, particularly longer-duration securities, as it leads to a decline in their prices, and results in mark-to-market losses for investors.   According to most debt mutual fund (MF) managers, the current strategy is to focus on accruals or carry (interest income), while waiting for the right opportunity to add duration through higher-duration government bonds.

“Our preference today is to earn carry at the shorter end, stay patient on duration, and use periods of yield repricing to gradually add duration when the risk-reward becomes more favourable,” Axis Mutual Fund said in a note on Wednesday.   Edelweiss MF and Bandhan MF shared a similar view. Also Read

Surplus liquidity may not persist beyond FY27: RBI Governor Malhotra

Bank margins set for near-term boost as EBLR loans reprice after MPC rise

A new policy cycle premium

Rupee closes at 96.78 per dollar as RBI policy fails to boost sentiment

“Interest rates generally peak out at the later stages of a rate-increase cycle. Until there is greater visibility on the peak in policy rates, investors should focus on accruals,” said Edelweiss MF.   “We remain conservatively to very conservatively positioned on duration risk across a host of our fixed-income funds. We will look closely for any signs of moderation in the global themes,” said Suyash Choudhary, chief investment officer – fixed income, Bandhan MF.

Wealth managers are also taking a cautious approach towards long-duration bonds and funds.   “Until there is greater visibility on inflation and the terminal policy rate, duration should, therefore, be avoided,” said Yogesh Kalwani, head of investments at InCred Wealth. “We recommend allocating up to 60 per cent of the fixed-income portfolio to accrual-oriented strategies, with average maturities of up to three years, providing relatively lower sensitivity to further rate increases while locking in attractive yields,” he added.   The fund manager preference is also currently in the shorter side of the yield curve.   "We see value in AAA-rated bonds maturing in two to three years and offering yields of around 7.75 per cent to 8.25 per cent," said Edelweiss MF.

"We prefer the one-three-year segment of the curve, particularly high-quality corporate bonds, where favourable carry, ample liquidity, and limited CD (certificate of deposit) issuance create an attractive risk-reward balance," Axis MF stated.                                                            Bonding it right Fund managers say they prefer AAA bonds over G-secs currently Cite better risk reward, especially in AAA bonds maturing within 3 years Possible open market operations, deferment of Bloomberg index inclusion and other macro risks cloud G-sec outlook

item.title: Apple's smart home push could test a market still struggling with adoption
item.description: Samsung SmartThings update and new local-control features come as Apple reportedly prepares a wider smart home push, while Matter and on-device processing aim to address compatibility and reliability ...
item.dc:creator: Harsh Shivam
item.content:encoded: Apple is reportedly preparing to make a bigger push into the smart home market, with a new home hub, an updated HomePod mini and a new Apple TV expected on October 13. A Bloomberg report also suggests that the company is working with LG on a range of connected home devices, including a smart doorbell, thermostat, deadbolt lock and security cameras. The move puts Apple more directly against Amazon, Google and Samsung, which already have connected home platforms spanning speakers, displays, televisions, appliances, cameras, thermostats and other devices. Apple’s reported plans also come as Samsung updates SmartThings with local device control and support for the latest Matter standard. The developments point to a market that has expanded in terms of available hardware, but has struggled to turn connected devices into a mainstream household purchase. ALSO READ: Apple partners with LG on doorbells, lock, thermostat in smart home pushSmart home market is growing, but at a slow paceData from International Data Corporation (IDC) shows that global smart home device shipments grew 0.6 per cent in 2024 before rising 4.4 per cent in 2025. The increase in 2025 suggests a recovery in shipments, but does not indicate a rapid expansion of the category. Market estimates also present a different picture when household penetration is considered. Market data platform Statista expects smart home household penetration to reach 82.1 per cent globally in 2026, with the market generating $159.5 billion in revenue. However, the same data puts average revenue per installed smart home at only $20.18. Statista calculates this by dividing smart home hardware revenue by the number of households with at least one active smart home device. The low average spending suggests that much of the market remains concentrated around individual devices rather than complete home automation systems. Having a smart device is not the same as having a connected home. A household with one smart bulb or plug can be counted as part of the smart home market. A more complete setup involving smart locks, thermostats, security cameras, sensors, lighting and a central controller costs far more.Why consumers have not adopted connected homes at scaleOne of the biggest problems has been that smart home devices have not always worked well across different platforms. Amazon, Google, Apple and Samsung have each built their own ecosystems, while device makers have historically relied on proprietary apps and connectivity standards. A consumer buying products from multiple brands could therefore end up managing several apps, accounts and hubs. The problem becomes more visible when automation is involved. A basic routine can depend on a device connecting to Wi-Fi, communicating with a cloud service and then sending an instruction to another device.ALSO READ: What happens when AI learns from info increasingly shaped by AI itself?Internet connectivity is another weak point. Cloud-dependent devices can become unavailable when the home internet connection goes down, even when the devices themselves are still powered. That is a bigger problem for products such as lights, locks and switches than it is for entertainment devices. Consumers expect a physical light switch or door lock to work without depending on an external server. Cost is another barrier. A smart plug or basic connected bulb can be inexpensive, but a larger installation involving cameras, locks, sensors, thermostats and a central hub can quickly become expensive. This leaves the market with a large number of individual smart devices but fewer households with fully connected homes.Matter has not removed the ecosystem problemMatter was introduced to address some of these compatibility issues by providing a common standard for smart home devices. Matter is essentially a universal, open-source smart home connectivity standard that allows devices from different manufacturers to work together securely and locally. The Connectivity Standards Alliance has continued to add device categories and capabilities to the standard but interoperability is still not the same as a common user experience. A Matter-compatible device can work with multiple platforms, but the features available can depend on the platform controlling it. Different versions of Matter also need to be supported by the hubs and controllers involved. The result can be a situation where a device is technically compatible with several ecosystems but does not offer the same functionality across them. Matter’s multi-admin feature was meant to solve some of these issues by allowing the same device to be controlled through more than one smart home platform. In theory, a light or sensor set up through Apple Home could also be shared with Google Home or Samsung SmartThings. But setting this up can still involve moving the device between ecosystems, scanning Matter pairing codes and dealing with connection or pairing failures. A common standard has made devices more compatible, but it has not made the setup process equally simple across platforms.Samsung is pushing more control into the homeSamsung’s latest SmartThings update addresses one of the more practical problems with connected homes: dependence on the cloud. When a smartphone and compatible SmartThings hub are connected to the same Wi-Fi network, the phone can now communicate directly with the hub instead of routing the command through Samsung’s cloud. Samsung says this can improve response times by about 30 per cent under controlled testing and allows connected devices to remain controllable during temporary internet disruptions. The update also adds support for Matter 1.6. This brings four new device categories to SmartThings, including energy meters, closures such as specialised doors and gates, irrigation systems and soil sensors. The change is significant for Samsung because SmartThings spans smartphones, televisions, appliances and dedicated hubs. The company is trying to make those devices function as controllers for a wider set of products rather than relying on each connected device to communicate with its own cloud service. Samsung’s approach also shows why local processing and control are becoming more important as smart homes expand. A connected home with dozens of devices generates a constant stream of commands and sensor data. Sending every action through the internet adds latency and creates another point of failure. However, it should be noted that local control does not remove cloud services from the smart home. Samsung’s system still switches to cloud-based remote control when a user is away from the home network. Older devices that depend on their manufacturers’ cloud servers can also remain unusable during an internet outage.Apple is entering a market that already has established platformsApple’s reported plans are broader than adding another smart speaker. The company is expected to introduce a smart home hub with a roughly six-inch display, alongside a refreshed HomePod mini and Apple TV. The hub is expected to act as a central interface for controlling connected devices and could use Apple’s updated Siri capabilities. Apple is also reportedly working with LG on devices including a video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt, temperature sensor and indoor, outdoor and floodlight cameras. The products are expected to work with Apple’s smart home ecosystem and support standards such as Matter and Thread. That gives Apple a route to expand beyond the limited number of first-party smart home products it has offered so far. The challenge is that Amazon and Google have been building their respective home platforms for years. Amazon has Echo speakers, Fire TV devices, a smart thermostat and Ring security products, while Google has Nest speakers, displays, cameras, doorbells and thermostats. Samsung has a different advantage. SmartThings can be used across Samsung televisions, smartphones and home appliances, giving the company a large installed base of devices that can also act as parts of a smart home system. Apple therefore enters the category with a large device ecosystem of its own, but not necessarily a corresponding lead in home automation hardware.The smart home is moving towards a central controllerThe smart home market is moving towards a model in which the central device does more than issue voice commands. Apple’s reported hub, Samsung’s SmartThings platform and products such as newer local smart home hubs from companies including UGREEN and Anker point towards a greater role for a central device that connects different hardware, processes information locally and manages automation. UGREEN’s HomeAgent hubs, for example, combine local storage, on-device AI and Matter-based device control. Anker’s MindBase takes a similar approach, combining local storage with processing for connected cameras and other smart home devices. The shift towards local processing also addresses one of the basic problems that has held back connected homes. A smart home needs to be reliable before consumers are willing to depend on it for everyday functions. Apple’s entry could bring more attention to the category, while Samsung’s latest SmartThings update shows that established players are still working on the basic infrastructure behind connected homes. The next phase of the smart home market may therefore depend less on how many new devices are launched and more on whether those devices can work together without adding complexity for households.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Finance / News / Individuals exempt from reporting foreign earnings; RBI to issue FAQs soon

Individuals exempt from reporting foreign earnings; RBI to issue FAQs soon Even in the case of entities, there is a provision for self-declaration up to a cap of ₹10 lakh per bill, Governor Sanjay Malhotra said

Reserve Bank of India | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India Mumbai 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 6:23 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Clarifying that individuals do not need to report imports or export earnings, the Reserve Bank on Wednesday said it will publish FAQs (frequently asked questions) shortly to quell "misunderstandings" around the recently implemented regulatory changes. Even in the case of entities, there is a provision for self-declaration up to a cap of ₹10 lakh per bill, Governor Sanjay Malhotra said. Malhotra said the unified Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, implemented from October 1, get services players on par with merchandise entities when it comes to reporting requirements. "...individuals are not included with respect to the reporting requirements for contracts of a personal nature. There seems to be some misunderstanding on the reporting obligations. We will clarify through an FAQ shortly," Deputy Governor Rohit Jain said.

He said the new regulations are aimed at simplification and promoting ease of doing business, and added that sufficient time was given to the members of trade as the guidelines were published in January this year. Malhotra also said that the reporting on the RBI platform is to be done by intermediaries, including banks or authorised dealers and not by the exporters or importers. "...we feel it is not a major inconvenience or a burden," he said, adding that some of the information was already being shared by the importers and exporters with the intermediaries.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
